Hi Dad,

Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: Why does a chatbot sometimes make things up so confidently? It is built to sound right, not to check whether it is right. The answer is at the end of this email.

  • The US Justice Department sets up a “Super Intelligence” task force. The US Justice Department has set up a “Super Intelligence Task Force” to pursue people who misuse AI, from foreign governments to fraudsters, and to press AI companies to keep strong internal controls. Despite the grand name, it is about today’s AI: since September, US agencies have been ordered to call AI “super intelligence”. The department has not said how large the unit is or how it will work with other agencies. Read more and the background.
  • How scientists actually use Claude (an Anthropic study). Anthropic, which makes Claude (the AI writing this email), studied about 207,000 research sessions and found scientists use Claude mostly to analyse data and write, and much less for coming up with ideas, even though scientists rank ideas as the most important part of their work. It is the company’s own study of its own product, based on two months of consumer accounts, and no outside group has checked it. Read more and the background.
  • Microsoft closes a 50-person AI research group. A prominent researcher, John Langford, says Microsoft has effectively shut down AI Frontiers, a roughly 50-person research group, after moving it into its product-focused AI division, which he says prefers making models bigger to doing research. He and the group’s other founding leaders have left. This is his account; I found no comment from Microsoft. Read more and the background.
  • An MIT model predicts how molecules behave from very little data. MIT researchers have released a free AI model, CheMeleon, that predicts how molecules will behave (how well they dissolve, for example) from only a handful of examples, so chemists need to make fewer molecules by trial and error. In a public contest, nine of the top 20 entries used it. Its advantage over other models comes from the authors’ own tests. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: A chipmaker says AI buyers are crowding everyone else out, Anthropic explains how its AI agents keep a memory, Thinking Machines releases a new model, with open weights promised, Can AI help scientists build explanations, not just fit data?.

Answer to the question of the day. A chatbot writes by guessing, word by word, what a good answer would most likely look like. Most of the time that guess matches the facts, because it learned from a huge amount of mostly accurate text. But it has no built-in way to look a fact up and check it, so when it does not really know, it still produces something that sounds plausible: an invented date, a book that does not exist, a court case nobody ever heard. People call these mistakes “hallucinations”. They happen less often when you give the chatbot clear context and tell it that “I don’t know” is an acceptable answer, but they have not been eliminated, so anything important (health, money, law) is worth checking elsewhere. The article below, written for general readers, explains the causes and what helps. Annet Sukhareva, “Why do neural networks hallucinate, and how can the problem be solved?” (T—Zh / Tinkoff Journal, 2024, in Russian).
